lesson.title: When Plugging In Fails: Indeterminate Forms
lesson.summary: An indeterminate form is an expression like 0 over 0 that direct substitution produces without revealing the actual value of the limit, since different functions that all substitute to the same form can have completely different limits.
lesson.body:
Direct substitution is a fast, reliable shortcut right up until it isn't. Sometimes plugging the target value into a function produces an expression that is not simply a well-defined number and not simply undefined in an obvious way either, like a nonzero number divided by 0. Instead it produces a form such as 0 divided by 0, infinity divided by infinity, infinity minus infinity, 0 times infinity, 0 raised to the 0, infinity raised to the 0, or 1 raised to the infinity. These are called indeterminate forms, and the name is precise: the form itself does not determine the answer. The actual limit behind an indeterminate form could turn out to be any finite number, could be infinite, or could fail to exist at all, depending entirely on the specific functions involved.

The reason these forms are genuinely ambiguous, rather than just inconvenient, is easiest to see with a small set of examples that all produce the identical 0 over 0 form at x equals 0, yet resolve to different answers. Consider the limit as x approaches 0 of x divided by x. For every x not equal to 0 this simplifies to 1, so the limit is 1, even though direct substitution at x equals 0 literally gives 0 over 0. Now consider the limit as x approaches 0 of x squared divided by x. This simplifies to x for every x not equal to 0, so the limit is 0, and yet substitution again gives 0 over 0. Finally consider the limit as x approaches 0 of x divided by x squared. This simplifies to 1 over x, which grows without bound as x approaches 0 from the right and plunges without bound from the left, so the two sided limit does not exist at all, despite substitution once again producing 0 over 0. Three expressions, the identical indeterminate form on substitution, and three different outcomes: 1, 0, and no limit at all. That is exactly what it means for a form to be indeterminate.

The crucial takeaway is that encountering an indeterminate form is not a dead end and does not mean the limit fails to exist. It means direct substitution has stopped being useful and some other technique is required to uncover the real behavior of the function near the point in question. Frequently that technique is algebraic: rewriting the expression in an equivalent form, valid everywhere near the point except possibly at the point itself, whose direct substitution does work cleanly.

Among the seven indeterminate forms listed above, two show up constantly in practice and are worth singling out for dedicated treatment. The 0 over 0 form arises whenever a numerator and denominator both vanish at the same point, which happens routinely with rational functions that share a common factor. The infinity over infinity form arises when both the numerator and denominator grow without bound, which happens routinely with rational functions as x heads toward infinity. Both of these are explored next, followed by the family of algebraic techniques, including factoring and rationalization, that resolve them.
